title: How do you build a training matrix for an airline?
description: Build an airline training matrix: crew checks, dispatcher and cabin crew recurrent training, dangerous goods, drug and alcohol programs and SMS by market.
shortAnswer: An airline training matrix is built by listing every operational function (flight crew, cabin crew, dispatchers, check pilots, cargo and ramp staff, passenger agents, safety managers) against the aviation authority rules in each country of operation, then recording for each cell the validity period, the month it expires, and the record an inspector will sample. Airline rules fix more intervals than most industries, so the matrix is largely a calendar of expiring qualifications.
keyTakeaways: Airline obligations are driven by function: crew position and aircraft type for pilots, acceptance and loading duties for dangerous goods, and safety sensitive status for drug and alcohol programs.
Unlike most regulated sectors, aviation rules set hard clocks: 6 and 12 calendar month checks for pilots, 24 month dangerous goods recurrence and 30 month drug and alcohol education in Australia.
Validity is counted in calendar months, often from the end of a month, so the matrix should store expiry months and grace rules rather than simple anniversary dates.
Evidence is specific: instructor certifications of proficiency, dangerous goods records kept at least 36 months, and Part 99 records kept five years.
Watch dates as at November 2026 include the 68th edition of the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations on 1 January 2027 and the end of CASA EX29/24 on 31 May 2027.

sections.heading: Why can an airline not use a generic compliance matrix?

blocks.text: Because most airline training is a condition of being allowed to operate a flight, not a policy preference, and the rules attach to positions, aircraft types and functions that a generic matrix does not model. A captain whose 6 month recurrent flight training lapses cannot legally fly as pilot in command, whatever the rest of their record says.

The general method in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) holds: people down one side, obligations across the top, a rule in each cell. An airline adds three dimensions: the aircraft type or group a person is qualified on, the market whose authority approved the program, and the expiry month for each check. Treat flight and cabin crew as [safety critical roles](/glossary/safety-critical-role) whose currency gates rostering.

sections.heading: Which training rules apply to airlines in each market?

blocks.text: Columns come from the authority that issued the air operator certificate and from every state where the airline handles cargo or employs safety sensitive staff. Each summary below draws only on the linked regulation page.

items: **United States.** A Part 121 carrier needs an FAA approved training program under Subpart N, with initial and final approval before use ([FAA Part 121 crewmember training](/regulations/faa-part-121-crewmember-training)). Crewmembers complete recurrent training within the preceding 12 calendar months, and pilots in command also complete recurrent flight training within the preceding 6 calendar months. Newly hired crewmembers and dispatchers receive 40 programmed hours of basic indoctrination, and emergency drills recur once each 24 calendar months. 14 CFR 5.91 requires SMS training for the accountable executive, management and employees identified in 5.23.

**United States, drug and alcohol.** Part 120 requires an Employee Assistance Program with education and initial training for safety sensitive employees, at least 60 minutes of initial training plus a recurrent program for supervisors who make reasonable cause drug testing decisions, and at least 60 minutes on alcohol misuse indicators for supervisors making reasonable suspicion decisions ([FAA drug and alcohol program](/regulations/faa-drug-and-alcohol-program-training)). Nine safety sensitive functions are covered, including flight crew, flight attendants, dispatchers, ground security coordinators and operations control specialists.

**United States, hazardous materials.** Air carrier hazmat training must have been completed within the past 24 months under 14 CFR 121.1005 ([IATA and ICAO dangerous goods](/regulations/iata-dangerous-goods-training-requirements)), and the general rule in 49 CFR 172.704 requires function specific, safety and security awareness training, with recurrent training at least every three years ([DOT hazmat](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training)).

**European Union.** Under ORO.FC.230 of Regulation (EU) No 965/2012, the operator proficiency check is valid for 6 calendar months, the line check and emergency and safety equipment training and checking for 12 calendar months, ground and flight training recurs at least every 12 calendar months, and CRM is delivered in modules across each 3 year period ([EU aircrew recurrent training](/regulations/eu-aircrew-recurrent-training-requirements)). Cabin crew complete annual recurrent training under ORO.CC.140, with practical elements every three years.

**Australia.** Part 99 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations requires AOC holders with safety sensitive staff to keep a drug and alcohol management plan whose education program each employee and DAMP supervisor attends before starting duties and then within 30 months of the last attendance ([CASA Part 99](/regulations/casa-part-99-drug-and-alcohol-management-plan-training)). CASA EX29/24 gives effect to two yearly dangerous goods training.

**Any market carrying cargo.** IATA DGR 1.5 requires the employer to ensure staff are competent before performing dangerous goods functions, with training covering general familiarization, function specific tasks and safety, based on functions rather than job titles.

sections.heading: Which airline intervals are fixed by rule and which does the carrier choose?

blocks.text: Most crew and dangerous goods intervals are fixed by rule, while drug and alcohol recurrence for US supervisors and SMS refreshers are left to the carrier. Record the source of each interval so an inspector can see which cells are legal limits and which are internal policy.

items: **Fixed by rule.** Pilot checks under ORO.FC.230; Part 121 recurrent training and the 6 month captain requirement; 24 calendar month emergency drills; 24 month dangerous goods recurrence; 30 month Part 99 education; three year DOT hazmat recurrence.

**Counted in calendar months.** EU validity periods are counted from the end of the month under ORO.FC.145, and 14 CFR 121.1005 treats training completed in the month before or after the due month as on time. 14 CFR 121.401(b) contains a grace month rule for Part 121 programs. Store the expiry month, not a day.

**Alternative programs change the clock.** Under ORO.FC.231, an approved evidence based training program of at least six modules over 3 years may replace ORO.FC.230 checks, and an ATQP may extend some validity periods after two years. The matrix must record which program each pilot is on.

**Left to the carrier.** Part 120 requires a reasonable recurrent program for reasonable cause supervisors but sets no interval, and 14 CFR 5.91 requires SMS training to attain and maintain competencies without a cycle. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) for documenting the rationale.

sections.heading: What training records will aviation inspectors ask for?

blocks.text: Expect requests for proof of competence for a named person on a named date, not a course list. Aviation records are tied to individual qualifications, and retention periods differ by rule.

items: **Crew training.** The instructor or check pilot certification of proficiency becomes part of the crewmember record under 14 CFR 121.401.

**Dangerous goods.** IATA DGR 1.5.1.4 sets record contents and retention for a minimum of 36 months from the most recent completion month. US air carriers keep records for the preceding 3 years while the person performs the function and for 90 days after, including test certification (14 CFR 121.1007).

**Drug and alcohol.** FAA alcohol training records, supervisor reasonable suspicion training documentation and training certification are kept for two years under 14 CFR 120.219. CASA Part 99 records are kept for five years and destroyed within six months after, and education attendance is reported for the 6 month periods ending 1 March and 1 September.
**General hazmat.** 49 CFR 172.704(d) requires a record covering the preceding three years with name, completion date, materials, trainer name and address and certification of training and testing.
Planning for an inspection is covered in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: Which airline training changes fall in 2026 and 2027?

blocks.text: Add these as dated rows so affected cells change on the right day. Each date comes from the linked regulation pages, as at November 2026.

items: **1 January 2027:** the 68th edition of the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations takes effect, incorporating the 2027 to 2028 Technical Instructions amendments, including a prohibition on power banks over 100 Wh and a limit of 2 power banks. Passenger handling and cabin crew content needs review.
**28 May 2027:** Part 135 operators and 91.147 letter of authorization holders must implement an SMS under 14 CFR 5.9, which matters for airline groups with regional or charter affiliates.
**31 May 2027:** CASA EX29/24, which gives effect to two yearly dangerous goods training in Australia, is repealed at the end of that day. Track what replaces it.

**20 December 2027:** Part 120 extends to Part 145 repair stations outside the United States that perform safety sensitive maintenance on Part 121 aircraft, unless recognized under 120.10, which affects contracted maintenance rows.

blocks.title: Already in force
blocks.text: EU pilots' rules were consolidated on 25 May 2026, and the EASA Easy Access Rules for Air Operations reached Revision 24 in March 2026. A US hazmat rule effective 13 February 2026 adjusted 172.704(e)(1) exceptions for packaging manufacturers.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each aviation obligation with the function, aircraft type and authority it belongs to, and links it to the learning outcomes and assessment points that demonstrate competence. When an authority amends a validity period or a new DGR edition is issued, the affected rows and materials are flagged for review. See [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence).

faqs.q: Should dangerous goods training be tracked by job title?
faqs.a: No. IATA DGR 1.5 and its competency based guidance assign training to functions, not job titles. A customer service agent who accepts checked baggage and a cargo agent who accepts consignments perform different functions, so tag each person with the functions they perform and attach the dangerous goods columns to those functions.

faqs.q: How should a matrix handle a pilot on an evidence based training program?
faqs.a: Record the program as an attribute of the pilot row. Under ORO.FC.231 an approved EBT program can substitute for the ORO.FC.230 checks, with at least six modules over three years, each valid for 12 months. A pilot on EBT therefore has different expiry columns from a pilot on the standard program.

faqs.q: Do contractors and ground handling agents belong in the airline's matrix?
faqs.a: Yes, where they perform regulated functions. CASA Part 99 education covers contractors, subcontractors and volunteers who perform safety sensitive aviation activities, and FAA safety sensitive functions include assistants and trainees. Ground handlers that accept or load dangerous goods also need DGR training, and the airline will want to see the evidence.

faqs.q: Can one dangerous goods record satisfy the FAA and IATA rules together?
faqs.a: Often, if it contains every required field. The DGR sets record contents and a 36 month minimum, while 14 CFR 121.1007 requires the preceding three years of training plus test certification, kept for 90 days after the person stops performing the function. Design one record that meets the longer and stricter of each.
